title: Bariatric Surgery: Post-Operative Monitoring and Supplementation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult after sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass attending a Saudi bariatric centre or primary health centre for long-term follow-up: monitoring schedule and blood tests, lifelong vitamin and mineral supplementation, how to recognise and treat iron, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D and thiamine deficiency, warning symptoms that need immediate treatment, and pregnancy advice. Uses the 2020 British Obesity and Metabolic Surgery Society guideline and a Riyadh one-year sleeve gastrectomy cohort, with UK product information for each medicine. Not for pre-operative selection, surgical complications such as leaks or strictures, adolescents (refer to specialists), or malabsorptive procedures (biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch) beyond brief notes.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery post-operative nutrition guideline was found; the pathway follows the 2020 British Obesity and Metabolic Surgery Society guideline written for the United Kingdom. Its recommendations are mostly grade D or good-practice points, i.e. expert opinion.

The Saudi source is a single prospective cohort at King Khalid University Hospital, Riyadh, of laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy patients over 12 months; it shows local deficiency patterns (35.7% iron deficient) but is small (28 participants) and descriptive.

Doses are taken from the British guideline and from United Kingdom summaries of product characteristics (electronic Medicines Compendium), because the guideline's products (Forceval, ferrous sulphate 200 mg, hydroxocobalamin 1 mg) are UK products; Saudi equivalents and strengths may differ.

Calcium: the guideline gives no supplement dose, only a total intake of 1,200 to 1,500 mg a day from food and supplements after sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass (quoted from another author); no calcium regimen is written. The sources note calcium citrate is preferred in people at risk of kidney stones and carbonate is taken with food.

Folic acid 5 mg a day for at least 4 months is the guideline's treatment of folate deficiency after excluding vitamin B12 deficiency; the product label for folic acid was not read for this topic and no folic acid regimen is written (see the antenatal topic for a 5 mg tablet label).

Vitamin D deficiency loading doses are not given in the guideline, which refers to the Royal Osteoporosis Society guidance; that guidance was not read and no loading regimen is written. Maintenance 2,000 to 4,000 IU a day is the guideline's figure.

Treatment of vitamin A, E and K deficiency (oral vitamin A 10,000 to 25,000 IU daily for 1 to 2 weeks; vitamin E 100 to 400 IU; vitamin K 1 to 2 mg) and the specifics for malabsorptive procedures are quoted in the guideline but no product label was read and no regimen is written; refer to the bariatric centre.

Intravenous thiamine: the guideline says to give it for people unable to tolerate oral thiamine or with suspected acute deficiency but gives no dose; the dose below is from the Pabrinex summary of product characteristics (2 to 3 pairs of ampoules every 8 hours) and local Wernicke's encephalopathy protocols should be used where they exist.

The guideline recommends oral thiamine 200 to 300 mg a day (or vitamin B co-strong 1 or 2 tablets three times a day) for people at risk; vitamin B co-strong was not checked against a label, and only thiamine hydrochloride 100 mg tablets are written.
Pregnancy, adolescents, biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch, one-anastomosis gastric bypass and the choice of vitamin D loading regimen are only touched on and need specialist input.
Protein supplementation, dietary advice, exercise and weight regain management were not part of the sources read in detail.
Figures were read by automated extraction of the guideline, the article and the product information; spot-check each dose against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: All bariatric procedures can cause clinically significant micronutrient deficiencies, and many people have low vitamin and mineral levels before surgery; lifelong nutritional monitoring is an essential part of care (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Summary). Iron deficiency anaemia is common because of low dietary iron, reduced intestinal absorption and, in some women, menstruation (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Haematinics). Vitamin B12 absorption needs an acidic environment and intrinsic factor from the stomach, so it falls after sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass; stores last about 2 years so deficiency can appear several years later and may cause irreversible neuropathy (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Haematinics). Thiamine deficiency can follow prolonged vomiting, rapid weight loss, poor intake or alcohol, and can progress to Wernicke's encephalopathy (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Thiamine). In 28 Riyadh patients after sleeve gastrectomy, intake of iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D stayed below recommended levels, 35.7% were iron deficient, and vitamin supplement use rose at 3 and 6 months but fell by 12 months (Riyadh sleeve gastrectomy nutrition study, Section Abstract).
keyMechanisms: All bariatric procedures can cause clinically significant micronutrient deficiencies, and many people have low vitamin and mineral levels before surgery; lifelong nutritional monitoring is an essential part of care (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Summary).
Iron deficiency anaemia is common because of low dietary iron, reduced intestinal absorption and, in some women, menstruation (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Haematinics).

Vitamin B12 absorption needs an acidic environment and intrinsic factor from the stomach, so it falls after sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass; stores last about 2 years so deficiency can appear several years later and may cause irreversible neuropathy (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Haematinics).

Thiamine deficiency can follow prolonged vomiting, rapid weight loss, poor intake or alcohol, and can progress to Wernicke's encephalopathy (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Thiamine).

In 28 Riyadh patients after sleeve gastrectomy, intake of iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D stayed below recommended levels, 35.7% were iron deficient, and vitamin supplement use rose at 3 and 6 months but fell by 12 months (Riyadh sleeve gastrectomy nutrition study, Section Abstract).

symptoms: Persistent vomiting, difficulty swallowing, poor oral intake or very fast weight loss (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Fatigue, breathlessness or pallor from anaemia (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Anaemia).
Numbness, tingling, unsteadiness, confusion or memory change (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

Night blindness or dry eyes (vitamin A), hair loss, taste change or poor wound healing (zinc or copper) (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Trace minerals: zinc, copper, selenium and magnesium).
Oedema (protein malnutrition) (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Protein malnutrition/protein–energy malnutrition/oedema).
physicalSigns: Ataxia, confusion, ophthalmoplegia or coma suggest Wernicke's encephalopathy (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Thiamine).
Peripheral neuropathy and ankle oedema (dry or wet beriberi) (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Thiamine).
Pallor, glossitis, hair loss (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Trace minerals: zinc, copper, selenium and magnesium).
redFlags: Prolonged vomiting, dysphagia, poor intake or fast weight loss: give thiamine immediately and refer back to the bariatric centre; do not wait for blood results (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3 and Table 5).
Confusion, ataxia or eye movement abnormality: treat as Wernicke's encephalopathy with intravenous thiamine and admit (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Sensory, motor or gait symptoms with possible vitamin B12 deficiency: treat immediately and seek urgent neurology and haematology advice (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Never give folic acid before vitamin B12 deficiency has been checked and treated (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Oedema or protein malnutrition: investigate and refer back to the bariatric centre (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Anaemia that does not respond to iron: look for blood loss and other deficiencies including zinc, copper and selenium (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
precipitants: Sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and malabsorptive procedures all carry deficiency risk, which is higher with malabsorptive operations (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Summary).
Menstruating women have higher iron needs (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).
Poor adherence: supplement use fell by 12 months in Riyadh (Riyadh sleeve gastrectomy nutrition study, Section Abstract).
Alcohol misuse, prolonged vomiting and poor dietary intake raise thiamine deficiency risk (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Low haemoglobin and low mean cell volume with serum ferritin under 15 µg/L; ferritin of 50 µg/L or higher can still be iron deficiency if inflammation is present (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Iron deficiency anaemia).
Macrocytic anaemia and neuropathy; can occur without anaemia; may be masked by folic acid (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Vitamin B12 and folate).
Macrocytic anaemia; suggests poor adherence or low intake (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Haematinics).

Anaemia, hair loss, taste change, neuromuscular abnormalities; zinc excess can cause copper deficiency (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Trace minerals: zinc, copper, selenium and magnesium).
Ataxia, confusion, ophthalmoplegia, neuropathy after vomiting or rapid weight loss (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Thiamine).

clinicalManagement.title: Set the follow-up plan
actions: Arrange follow-up within the bariatric service for at least 2 years, with specialist dietetic support and nutritional assessment (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
After discharge arrange nutritional monitoring at least yearly for life in shared care (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Record the operation type, because monitoring and supplements depend on it (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Postoperative care and biochemical monitoring).

clinicalManagement.title: Start lifelong supplements
actions: Give a complete multivitamin and mineral supplement with thiamine, iron, selenium, zinc and copper daily after every procedure (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).

Add elemental iron (ferrous sulphate 200 mg daily, twice daily if menstruating), vitamin B12 injections every 3 months, and vitamin D3 2,000 to 4,000 IU daily (see medicines) (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).
Ensure good dietary calcium; take iron and calcium 2 hours apart; calcium carbonate with food and citrate with or without food (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).
Consider oral thiamine for the first 3 to 4 months (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).

clinicalManagement.title: Check bloods on schedule
actions: Full blood count, ferritin, folate, vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium, renal and liver function; zinc and copper at least yearly (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Check HbA1c if diabetic and lipids if dyslipidaemic (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Ask about supplement adherence at every visit, because use fell by 12 months in Riyadh (Riyadh sleeve gastrectomy nutrition study, Section Abstract).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat thiamine risk or deficiency at once
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Immediately; do not wait for tests
actions: For vomiting, dysphagia, poor intake, fast weight loss, alcohol misuse or oedema give oral thiamine 200 to 300 mg daily (see medicines) and refer back to the bariatric centre (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3 and Table 5).
If unable to take oral doses or if Wernicke's encephalopathy is suspected give intravenous thiamine and admit (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Treat other deficiencies
clinicalManagement.timeframe: When a blood test is abnormal
actions: Iron deficiency anaemia: look for blood loss and treat per local iron deficiency guidance (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

Vitamin B12 deficiency: hydroxocobalamin 1 mg intramuscularly on alternate days if neurological symptoms until no further improvement, otherwise three times a week for 2 weeks, then every 2 to 3 months for life (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Folate deficiency: treat only after checking and treating vitamin B12 deficiency (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Low vitamin D: check adherence, then follow local or Royal Osteoporosis Society replacement guidance; refer if still deficient (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Low zinc and copper: consider two Forceval capsules daily for 3 months and recheck (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

clinicalManagement.title: Counsel on pregnancy
actions: Advise avoiding pregnancy for 12 to 18 months after surgery (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
Offer folic acid before conception and screen nutrition each trimester; refer to specialist antenatal care (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

regimens.indication: Prevention of micronutrient deficiency after bariatric surgery
regimens.dose: 1 capsule daily, preferably 1 hour after meals; do not exceed the stated dose (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2); the guideline notes that two capsules daily may be needed for mild zinc and copper deficiency (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5). Dilution and preparation: none; swallow whole with water.
regimens.duration: Lifelong after bariatric surgery, reviewed regularly (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4)
adjustments: Not recommended under 12 years (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2).
Do not add other vitamin or mineral supplements except under medical supervision (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Contains 4.5 mg beta-carotene; consider risks in current smokers and people exposed to asbestos (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).

May be used in pregnancy at the physician's recommendation; the guideline suggests switching to a preconception or pregnancy-specific supplement with beta-carotene instead of retinol (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.6; BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Adherence at every visit (Riyadh sleeve gastrectomy nutrition study, Section Abstract).
Blood tests per schedule (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Allergic reaction to soya or peanut (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
contraindications: Hypercalcaemia (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Haemochromatosis and other iron storage disorders (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Hypersensitivity to any ingredient; contains soya bean oil, so not for people allergic to peanut or soya (Forceval summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).

regimens.indication: Prevention of iron deficiency after sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass
regimens.dose: 200 mg ferrous sulfate (one tablet) daily; twice daily in menstruating women; adjust to blood results (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4; Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2: prophylactic dose one tablet daily, therapeutic one tablet 2 to 3 times daily). Dilution and preparation: none; swallow whole with water, do not suck or chew.
regimens.route: Oral, before or during meals depending on tolerance (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2)
regimens.frequency: Once daily, or twice daily in menstruating women
regimens.duration: Long term, guided by ferritin and haemoglobin
adjustments: Take with citrus fruit, citrus drinks or vitamin C; take calcium and iron 1 to 2 hours apart (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).
Absorption is reduced by tea, coffee, milk, antacids, zinc and calcium; give iron at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after these (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.5).
Separate from levothyroxine by 2 hours and from tetracyclines, quinolones and bisphosphonates (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.5).
Caution in swallowing difficulty because aspiration can cause bronchial necrosis (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Full blood count and ferritin at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Constipation, black stools, gastrointestinal irritation (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.8).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any ingredient (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Repeated blood transfusions (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Concomitant parenteral iron (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Haemochromatosis and other iron overload (Ferrous sulfate summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).

regimens.indication: Prevention of vitamin B12 deficiency after sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after sleeve gastrectomy, gastric bypass or malabsorptive surgery
regimens.dose: 1 mg (1 mL) every 3 months (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4); the summary of product characteristics gives 1,000 micrograms every 2 or 3 months for prophylaxis after gastrectomy or malabsorption (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2). Dilution and preparation: none; use the solution as supplied.
regimens.route: Intramuscular injection (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2)
adjustments: Do not use for megaloblastic anaemia of pregnancy (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.6).
Confirm the diagnosis in suspected deficiency before treating; folate deficiency may be masked (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Anticoagulated patients may need a deep subcutaneous alternative per local policy; not assessed in the sources.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Vitamin B12 and full blood count at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Plasma potassium during initial treatment of deficiency because hypokalaemia has been reported (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Allergy and anaphylaxis (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.8).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to hydroxocobalamin or any excipient (Hydroxocobalamin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).

regimens.indication: Maintenance of vitamin D after sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass
regimens.dose: 2,000 to 4,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily to keep serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D at 75 nmol/L or higher (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4); one 4,000 IU tablet is the daily maximum of the product (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2). Dilution and preparation: none; swallow whole or crush; may be taken with food.
regimens.duration: Lifelong, adjusted to 25-hydroxyvitamin D and calcium
adjustments: Do not exceed 4,000 IU a day from this product; count vitamin D from other sources (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2 and Section 4.4).
Use with caution in renal impairment, sarcoidosis, and with cardiac glycosides or diuretics; monitor calcium and creatinine (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Higher doses may be needed after malabsorptive procedures (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D and calcium at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Urine calcium if prone to stones (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
contraindications: Hypercalcaemia or hypercalciuria (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Hypervitaminosis D (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).
Hypersensitivity to any ingredient (Desunin summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).

regimens.indication: Prevention or treatment of thiamine deficiency after bariatric surgery
regimens.patientGroup: Adults at risk of or with mild to moderate thiamine deficiency
regimens.dose: 200 to 300 mg daily in divided doses for people with dysphagia, vomiting, poor intake or fast weight loss (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4 and Table 5); the summary of product characteristics gives 100 mg three times daily for severe deficiency and 50 mg daily for mild deficiency (Thiamine summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2). Dilution and preparation: none.
regimens.route: Oral (Thiamine summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2)
regimens.duration: Until intake is restored, then as advised by the bariatric team
adjustments: Contains lactose; avoid in galactose intolerance, Lapp lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption (Thiamine summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Thiosemicarbazone and fluorouracil can neutralise thiamine (Thiamine summary of product characteristics, Section 4.5).
Change to intravenous thiamine if vomiting persists or neurological signs appear (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

monitoring: Neurological signs: ataxia, confusion, eye movement abnormality (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Thiamine).
Oral intake and weight (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to thiamine or any excipient (Thiamine summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).

regimens.useWhen: Patient can swallow and keep down tablets, no neurological signs

regimens.indication: Rapid treatment of severe thiamine and vitamin B and C depletion, including suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after bariatric surgery with neurological signs or inability to take oral thiamine
regimens.genericName: Pabrinex (vitamin B and C) intravenous high potency concentrate for solution for infusion
regimens.dose: 2 to 3 pairs of 5 mL ampoules (one pair is ampoule 1 plus ampoule 2) every 8 hours, or at the physician's discretion (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2). Dilution and preparation: add equal volumes of ampoules 1 and 2 to 50 to 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% glucose and infuse over 30 minutes; inspect for particles; dilute before use (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.2 and Section 4.4).
regimens.route: Intravenous infusion over 30 minutes; for intravenous use only (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4)
regimens.duration: As directed by a physician until clinical improvement, then oral thiamine; admission is advised (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5)
adjustments: Rare anaphylaxis is possible, but it should not prevent use in people at risk of Wernicke's encephalopathy (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Early warning signs are sneezing or mild asthma; facilities to treat anaphylaxis must be available (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Give glucose after, not before, thiamine in people at risk of Wernicke's encephalopathy (not stated in the sources read; follow local protocol).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Anaphylaxis during and after the infusion (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.4).
Neurological recovery, vital signs, electrolytes, magnesium and glucose (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to the active substances or any excipient (Pabrinex summary of product characteristics, Section 4.3).

branches.entryCriteria: Adult after sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, started from the first postoperative weeks and continued for life, adjusted by blood results.

branches.label: Suspected or established thiamine deficiency after bariatric surgery
branches.entryCriteria: Adult after bariatric surgery with prolonged vomiting, dysphagia, poor oral intake, rapid weight loss, alcohol misuse, oedema, neuropathy or neurological symptoms, with no known allergy to thiamine preparations.

medicationPlan.note: Six medicines are written from the 2020 British guideline: four for routine supplementation after sleeve gastrectomy or gastric bypass (complete multivitamin and mineral, iron, vitamin B12, vitamin D3) and two alternatives for thiamine. Doses follow the guideline, and the preparation, administration, cautions and contraindications are from the United Kingdom summaries of product characteristics named in each row. All doses are for adults. SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: At least 2 years in the bariatric surgery service, then at least annual lifelong monitoring in shared care (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).

Full blood count, ferritin, folate, vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, calcium, renal and liver function at 3, 6 and 12 months in the first year, then at least annually (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D of 75 nmol/L or higher (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 3).
Serum ferritin under 15 µg/L with low haemoglobin and mean cell volume (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Section Iron deficiency anaemia).
Daily complete multivitamin and mineral supplement with thiamine, iron, selenium, zinc and copper after all procedures (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 4).
Avoid pregnancy for 12 to 18 months after surgery (BOMSS 2020 bariatric nutrition guideline, Table 5).

teaching.scope: Adult after sleeve gastrectomy or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass attending a Saudi bariatric centre or primary health centre for long-term follow-up: monitoring schedule and blood tests, lifelong vitamin and mineral supplementation, how to recognise and treat iron, vitamin B12, folate, vitamin D and thiamine deficiency, warning symptoms that need immediate treatment, and pregnancy advice. Uses the 2020 British Obesity and Metabolic Surgery Society guideline and a Riyadh one-year sleeve gastrectomy cohort, with UK product information for each medicine. Not for pre-operative selection, surgical complications such as leaks or strictures, adolescents (refer to specialists), or malabsorptive procedures (biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch) beyond brief notes.
learningObjectives: Plan lifelong follow-up with blood tests at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly.
Prescribe a complete multivitamin and mineral, iron, vitamin B12 and vitamin D for life.
Treat thiamine risk immediately without waiting for tests.
Check vitamin B12 before giving folic acid.
pitfalls: Waiting for blood results before giving thiamine.
keyPoints: Folic acid alone can mask vitamin B12 deficiency and precipitate spinal cord damage.
Deficiency may appear years after surgery.
Iron and calcium compete for absorption.

patientEducation: You will need vitamins and minerals every day for the rest of your life after weight-loss surgery.
Do not stop your supplements even when you feel well; many people stop after a year.
Take iron and calcium at different times, and take iron with vitamin C or citrus.
Tell us at once if you are vomiting for more than a day, cannot eat, or feel confused or unsteady.
Avoid pregnancy for 12 to 18 months after surgery and talk to us before you plan a pregnancy.
lifestyleAndDiet: Eat protein first and small regular meals as advised by your dietitian.
mdtReferrals: Bariatric surgeon; bariatric physician; specialist dietitian; primary care physician; clinical pharmacist; psychologist; endocrinologist; antenatal team for pregnancy; neurologist and haematologist for neurological or severe haematological problems.
dischargeCriteria: Operation type recorded; list and doses of supplements given; blood test schedule; named service for 2 years then annual shared care; warning symptoms that need same-day review (persistent vomiting, confusion, unsteadiness, numbness).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Blood tests at 3, 6 and 12 months then at least yearly for life, with supplement review at each visit; within the bariatric service for at least 2 years.
